query: For steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to corrosion? generation.hypothesis: The local chemical order in high-entropy alloys (HEAs) enhances their corrosion resistance by promoting the formation of a stable passivation film, which reduces the mobility of irradiation-induced interstitials and vacancies, thereby facilitating their recombination and reducing damage accumulation.

cited_evidence.text: SignificanceHigh-entropy alloys have emerged as promising structural materials for nuclear applications. Among the structural features of high-entropy alloys that may influence their irradiation response, a variable that has not received careful study so far is the internal local chemical order. By combining ion irradiation experiments and atomistic simulation of CrCoNi medium-entropy alloy, here we demonstrate that increased local chemical order (e.g., via thermal aging) significantly enhances their resistance to irradiation damage by narrowing the mobility ratio of irradiation-induced interstitials and vacancies that can facilitate their recombination. This finding opens an avenue to tailor radiation resistance, especially effective as the local chemical order are well suited to affect the evolution of point defects. High- (and medium-) entropy alloys have emerged as potentially suitable structural materials for nuclear applications, particularly as they appear to show promising irradiation resistance. High-entropy (HEAs) and medium-entropy (MEAs) alloys, denoted as M/HEAs, have attracted considerable attention due to their exceptional mechanical properties (, ) and corrosion resistance (, ). Recent studies have also demonstrated that M/HEAs have potential to be used as candidate materials for advanced nuclear applications since they exhibit improved irradiation resistance (). To date, both experimental studies and atomistic simulations have been carried out to investigate the irradiation behavior of M/HEAs. Specifically, extensive experimental studies have focused on tuning chemical complexities to enhance radiation tolerance in concentrated solid-solution alloys, by varying the number, the type, and the concentration of principal elements (). Manipulation of these constituent elements can provide an effective approach to alter the lattice distortion and consequently control the process of defect production and recombination, which could ultimately suppress damage accumulation. Early research reported that stainless steel, Fe-Cr alloy, and CrFe15Ni15 alloy have excellent corrosion resistance due to the dense Cr2O3 passivation film formed on the surface [,,]. Similarly, it was speculated that the Cr2O3 passivation film has the same effect in the corrosion resistance of HEAs. AlCoCrFeNi [], AlxCrFe1.5MnNi0.5 [], and Al0.5CoCrCuFeNiBx [] verified the foregoing speculation. Therefore, for the (CoCrFeNi)95Nb5 HEA coating passivation film of this study, it can be obtained from the results of XPS that the Cr2O3 in the passivation film provides good corrosion resistance for the coating, and the addition of trace amount of Nb results in forming a stable metal oxide of Nb2O5 in the passivation film of the coating, which also plays a positive role in the corrosion resistance [,].

As a well-known high-entropy alloys (HEA), equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi alloy, also known as Cantor alloy, has been increasingly investigated in recent years, with a focus on enhanced fracture toughness and ductility at cryogenic temperatures []. HEAs could become future materials for structural applications due to these superior properties. However, compared with the mechanical properties, the corrosion properties, which are also important for structural applications, have not been investigated to the same extent. The majority of HEAs, as represented by Cantor alloy, have a higher amount of Cr and Ni compared to commercial stainless steels (SS) such as AISI304, so that they are expected to exhibit high corrosion resistance, and they have been demonstrated to possess high passivating capability in neutral solutions [,,,,,]. However, it seems that the corrosion resistance of HEAs is not necessarily as high as expected given the large Cr and Ni content [,,], and in particular the pitting corrosion resistance in chloride-containing environments is inferior to AISI304 [,,]. In the studied CoCrFeMnNi alloys, the amount of Cr had a strong effect on the electrochemical behavior, and the passivity became more stable with increasing amounts of Cr. This higher pitting potential in NaCl solution and greater protective properties of passivation films in H2SO4 with a higher amount of Cr has been established in binary Fe–Cr alloys and stainless steels. However, in spite of extensive reports of enhanced corrosion resistance in UFG Fe–Cr alloys, in the present study, the effect of UFG formation on the corrosion resistance was less than expected; UFG formation via HPT of CoCrFeMnNi had little or no impact on the corrosion behavior.

decision.trend: Research on high-entropy alloys (HEAs) has shown promising results for corrosion resistance in various applications, including chemical-processing and nuclear-power. The trend suggests that HEAs can be designed to exhibit improved corrosion resistance through the manipulation of their composition, microstructure, and local chemical order. Studies have demonstrated that certain HEAs, such as CoCrFeNiMo0.85 and AlTiVNb, exhibit excellent corrosion resistance in different environments. The use of computational modeling and simulation has also been shown to be effective in predicting the properties of HEAs and optimizing their composition for improved corrosion resistance.
decision.unsolved: Despite the promising results, there is still a need to understand the underlying mechanisms of corrosion resistance in HEAs and to develop a mechanistic hypothesis that can explain their behavior. Additionally, the effects of local chemical order on the irradiation-induced defect evolution in HEAs need to be further investigated to tailor radiation resistance.
decision.lever: investigating the effect of local chemical order on corrosion resistance
decision.why: The next step would be to investigate the effect of local chemical order on corrosion resistance in HEAs, as this has been shown to be a critical factor in their irradiation response. By manipulating the local chemical order through thermal aging or other means, researchers can gain a deeper understanding of the underlying mechanisms of corrosion resistance in HEAs and develop more effective strategies for improving their performance in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications.
